chapters.title: Chapter 5: Beyond Markowitz: Fixing Mean-Variance Optimization

lessons.title: Factor-Based Portfolio Construction: Beyond Just Risk and Return

children.text: CAPM, back in Chapter 4, was already a factor model, just with exactly one factor: the market. This closing lesson of the chapter asks the obvious next question. If one systematic driver of return exists, are there others, and can naming them explicitly solve Lesson 1's estimation problem at the same time?

body.text: Decades of research have found a small number of other persistent, systematic drivers of stock returns beyond market beta. Pricing them in explicitly does two things at once: it captures return patterns CAPM alone misses, and it collapses the covariance matrix's parameter explosion from Chapter 2 into something genuinely estimable.

children.text: Eugene Fama and Kenneth French found, in a well-known pair of papers published in 1992 and 1993, that market beta alone left real, persistent patterns in average stock returns unexplained. Adding two more factors, a size factor (smaller companies tending to outperform larger ones) and a value factor (statistically cheap stocks, by measures like book-to-market, tending to outperform expensive ones), explained considerably more of the cross-section of returns than CAPM's single factor. Mark Carhart added a fourth, momentum, in 1997: stocks that have recently outperformed tending to keep outperforming over the following months. Fama and French later extended their own model to five factors in 2015, adding profitability and investment intensity.

body.caption: A K-factor expected return model. CAPM is the special case where K = 1 and the only factor is the market.

children.text: Worked Example: Three Factors for Five Familiar Stocks
Alongside each stock's market beta from Chapter 4, illustrative value and momentum exposures, plus illustrative annual factor premiums, market 9.3%, value 3%, momentum 4%, on top of Rf = 6.5%:

body.caption: Factor exposures and resulting expected returns (illustrative)

body.text: Maruti Suzuki's factor-model return, 21.13%, sits well above its CAPM figure, driven by positive value and momentum tilts on top of its already-high market beta: a cyclical auto stock with both a value and a momentum edge, in this illustration. HUL moves the opposite way, 9.89% versus CAPM's 11.49%, dragged down by negative value and momentum exposures consistent with a defensive, richly-valued, low-momentum FMCG name. CAPM would have priced both stocks using market beta alone and missed both effects entirely.

children.text: The Other Reason Factor Models Matter: Fewer Parameters

Chapter 2, Lesson 3 showed a 50-stock covariance matrix needs 1,275 separately estimated numbers. A factor model sidesteps almost all of that, because two stocks' covariance can be reconstructed entirely from their shared factor exposures and a small factor-level covariance matrix, plus each stock's own leftover, stock-specific variance. Instead of estimating every pair directly, you estimate K exposures per stock, K x (K+1) / 2 factor covariances, and N idiosyncratic variances.

body.caption: Parameters needed: full covariance matrix versus a K-factor model

body.text: At 500 stocks, a 3-factor model needs about 1.6% of the parameters a full covariance matrix requires. This is not a minor efficiency gain, it is the difference between an estimation problem that is realistic to solve reliably and one that Chapter 2 already showed becomes hopeless at real institutional scale, where a handful of noisy or wrong correlations can quietly corrupt the entire matrix.

children.text: Factor exposure is directly investable on NSE without building anything from scratch. Index families like Nifty200 Momentum 30, Nifty500 Value 50, Nifty Alpha 50, Nifty Quality 30, and Nifty Low Volatility 50 are each built to tilt toward one specific, well-documented factor, and are tracked by several Indian index funds and ETFs. A factor-aware investor can combine these in place of, or alongside, a plain market-cap-weighted Nifty 50 fund.
The Catch: Factors Are Not Free Money

body.text: Unlike the market risk premium, a factor premium is not remotely guaranteed to show up on any given year, or even decade. Value investing famously underperformed growth for an extended stretch through much of the 2010s globally, a real, well-documented drawdown, not a hypothetical risk. Factors can also become crowded as more capital chases them, eroding the very outperformance that drew attention to them in the first place. Finance researchers have proposed hundreds of purported factors in academic papers, a phenomenon economist John Cochrane termed the "factor zoo" in a widely cited 2011 address, and a large share of them likely reflect statistical data-mining rather than a genuine, persistent, economically sensible driver of returns. Market, value, size, momentum, quality, and low-volatility have the most robust evidence behind them. Most of the rest deserve real skepticism.

body.title: Apply the factor formula
body.prompt: A stock has a market beta of 1.2, a value beta of 0.5, and a momentum beta of -0.3. Using this lesson's factor premiums (market 9.3%, value 3%, momentum 4%) and Rf = 6.5%, what is its factor-model expected return?

body.title: Why fewer parameters
body.question: Why does a 3-factor model need dramatically fewer parameters than a full covariance matrix, for the same 100 stocks?
options: Because factor models simply ignore most of the stocks in the universe
Because every pair of stocks' covariance can be reconstructed from their shared factor exposures and a small factor covariance matrix, instead of each pair needing its own separately estimated number
Because factor models assume all stocks are perfectly correlated with each other
Because factor premiums are always equal to zero, removing the need to estimate them
body.explanation: A factor model explains covariance THROUGH a small set of shared exposures and a compact factor-level covariance matrix, rather than requiring every individual pair of stocks to be estimated directly. That structural shortcut is what shrinks 5,050 parameters down to a few hundred for 100 stocks.

cards.definition: Mean-variance optimization's tendency to concentrate weight in whichever asset has the highest ESTIMATED return, regardless of how reliable that estimate is.
Blends market-implied equilibrium returns with an investor's own confidence-weighted views, instead of using raw historical averages.
Builds a portfolio so every asset contributes equally to total risk, using only the covariance matrix and no expected-return input at all.
Explains returns and covariances through a small number of shared, systematic drivers (market, value, size, momentum, quality), reducing the number of parameters that must be separately estimated.

points: CAPM is a one-factor model. Fama and French's work, later extended by Carhart and others, showed additional systematic factors, size, value, momentum, quality, meaningfully improve on market beta alone.
Applied to five familiar stocks, factor-model returns diverged noticeably from CAPM for Maruti Suzuki and HUL, driven by value and momentum tilts CAPM cannot see.

Beyond improving on CAPM's accuracy, factor models solve Chapter 2's parameter explosion directly: a 3-factor model needs about 206 parameters for 50 stocks, versus 1,275 for a full covariance matrix.
Factor exposure is directly investable in India through NSE index families like Nifty200 Momentum 30, Nifty500 Value 50, and Nifty Alpha 50.
Factor premiums are not guaranteed the way the broad market premium is assumed to be, and can underperform for a decade or more, as value investing did through much of the 2010s.

This closes Chapter 5's three fixes for Markowitz's fragility: Black-Litterman anchors returns to equilibrium, risk parity avoids return estimation altogether, and factor models structurally reduce how much needs estimating in the first place. Chapter 6 turns to the real-world constraints, no short-selling, position limits, turnover, that shape how any of these get implemented in an actual portfolio.
